messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi had always known hardship, growing up in a rural African village where his family struggled to make ends meet. But it was what he witnessed at home, not the poverty or hunger, that had left an indelible mark on his life. His father's brutal beatings of his mother, the sound of her screams still echoing in his mind, had taught Kofi that safety was a myth. Even now, as a 45-year-old agricultural worker with a partner and a stable home, he couldn't shake off the feeling of being constantly on guard. As a child, Kofi would often hide under the bed or in the bushes outside, watching as his father's rage unfolded before him. He had always felt helpless, unable to intervene or protect his mother. This sense of powerlessness had grown into a crippling guilt over the years – "I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened," he would often say, his eyes clouding with tears. This inaction guilt was closely tied to his lost faith in people and life itself; Kofi had come to believe that no one was truly safe, that even those who seemed kind could turn violent at any moment. This negative appraisal of the world around him fuelled his threat monitoring – he was constantly hypervigilant, scanning his surroundings for potential dangers. At night, when the darkness outside seemed to press in on him, Kofi would lie awake, his senses heightened as he listened for any sign of movement or disturbance. He couldn't trust that he was safe, even with his partner by his side; "Even when others tell me I am safe," he said, shaking his head, "I find it impossible to believe it." As a result, Kofi had developed some maladaptive strategies to cope with this pervasive sense of threat. He would often ruminate about revenge against his father, fantasizing about ways to make him pay for what he had done. These thoughts consumed him at times, making it difficult for him to focus on work or engage with loved ones. Kofi also made sure never to be alone with another person, always seeking out the company of others as a way to feel safer. And when memories of his childhood threatened to surface, he would try hard not to think about them, suppressing thoughts and emotions that felt too overwhelming. However, these strategies had an unintended consequence – they reinforced Kofi's negative appraisals of himself and the world. By constantly replaying scenarios of revenge in his mind, Kofi perpetuated a cycle of anger and resentment that made it difficult for him to find peace. His inability to trust others or feel safe even in his own home eroded what little faith he had left in humanity. And by suppressing memories rather than confronting them, Kofi prevented himself from processing the trauma and moving forward. As time went on, this cycle of threat monitoring, maladaptive strategies, and negative appraisals tightened its hold on Kofi's life. His partner grew concerned about his increasingly withdrawn behaviour, and his performance at work began to suffer as he struggled to focus. It was only when Kofi realized that he couldn't keep living in a state of constant fear and hypervigilance that he finally sought help. He knew it wouldn't be easy – the wounds of his childhood ran deep – but he hoped that with therapy, he might begin to rebuild some semblance of trust and happiness.
